provenance.note: Hand-written ground truth for the historical-fault extraction channel (M13 channel B). Each incidentText is written to sound like a real support ticket or post-mortem while naming exactly one fault, so the expected record is decidable from the text alone. No incident text here is copied from any corpus: this file is authored, reviewable, and small. It exists so the M1 exit condition has a denominator that does not move when the model changes. The key grew from 19 to 30 samples in v2.45: at 19 the strict rate moved in 5.3-point steps, which is coarse against a 70% threshold, and the margin over it was one sample.
provenance.authoringRule: The expected.type must be derivable from the incident text by a careful human reader. A sample whose answer needs context the text does not carry is a bad sample, not a hard one.
provenance.annotationRule: The expected.component must be the deployed workload that owns the fault, and it must be recoverable from the incident text under the token rule the extraction prompt states -- every hyphen-delimited token of the name appears in the text, case-insensitively. This is asserted over the whole file in fault-prompt-grammar.test.ts, so an annotation that names something its text does not carry fails a test. One sample was re-annotated under this rule: config-feature-flag-checkout named `checkout-ui`, which its text never carries; see its annotationNote.
provenance.categoryRule: The expected.category must be the value inferFaultCategory (packages/core/src/fault/category.ts) returns for the sample's own expected.type. The rule is stated here because it was true of the whole file and written down nowhere: the category was authored by reading the type, so the derivation reproduces it exactly in every sample -- 30 of 30 in fault/category-derivation.test.ts, which asserts it over the whole file and asserts that every one of them lands on a member of FAULT_CATEGORIES, so an expected.type added without a derivable category fails a test rather than being counted as a miss. The same module measures the rule's discriminating power and records that it is below the floor, so this concordance is self-consistency and not a result: see finding 102. Whether the extraction prompt should state the rule is a product decision, deliberately not taken here.

samples.incidentText: Pager fired at 02:14 UTC: checkout-api p99 latency went from 180ms to 4.3s over eleven minutes. Container CPU throttling counters climbed the whole time and the pod sat pinned at its 500m limit. The load generator was unchanged from the previous week. Restarting the pod cleared it for about twenty minutes, then it returned. No error rate change in the downstream payment service.

The recommendation service has OOMKilled every 6 to 8 hours for three days. Heap dumps show the session cache growing without bound; entries are written and never evicted. RSS climbs from 400Mi to the 2Gi limit and the kernel kills the container. Traffic is flat. Rolling back last Tuesday's release stops the growth.

The log collector pod stopped accepting writes at 09:41. /var/lib/collector is at 100% usage; the retention job that should trim segments older than 24h has not run since the collector was rescheduled onto a node with a smaller data volume. Writes now fail with ENOSPC and the agent is dropping batches.

Cart-to-inventory calls got slow after the network policy change. Client-side span duration rose from 12ms to 900ms while the inventory service's own server-side handler time stayed at 11ms, so the time is being spent on the wire. No packet loss and no retransmits. The two services are now scheduled in different availability zones.

Roughly 8% of calls from the order service to the payment gateway time out at 3s. tcpdump on the client side shows SYN retransmissions; the gateway's own metrics show it received far fewer requests than the client sent. The egress interface on the client node reports a rising drop counter. Retries succeed when they land on a different node.

The search cluster split into two sides at 03:02 and each side elected its own leader. Queries on one side returned documents that the other side had already deleted. The split healed at 03:19 when the inter-node links came back. Nothing in the application changed; the only upstream event was a switch firmware roll on the rack carrying the third node.

The user-profile pod was terminated without a shutdown hook at 14:07 and a fresh one took 40 seconds to become ready, during which every request 503'd. Node conditions were healthy and memory was well under the limit, so this was the kubelet acting on an eviction decision made for a different workload on the same node. No application exception was logged because the process never got to handle a signal.

The media-transcoder container has restarted 178 times in 12 hours. Each start logs a segmentation fault in the native ffmpeg binding within two seconds of receiving the first job, before the HTTP listener comes up, so no probe ever passes. Liveness probes are not the cause: the exits all predate the probe window.

Cache GETs against the session Redis went from 0.4ms to 55ms at 21:30 and stayed there. The Redis instance itself reports a single command thread saturated at 100%; the SLOWLOG shows a KEYS command issued every 30 seconds by an unrelated debugging script. Application-side connection pool utilisation is normal, so clients are not the bottleneck.

Consumer group order-events accumulated 4.2 million messages of lag over six hours. The consumers are alive and polling, but their per-message processing time tripled after a schema change added a synchronous outbound call per record. Broker-side throughput is unchanged and the topic has spare partitions, so this is consumer-side throughput, not broker capacity.

The billing service began throwing 'connection pool exhausted' after the replica promotion. Pool size is 20 and all 20 are held by threads waiting on a lock held by a transaction that is itself waiting for a connection, so no thread can make progress. Postgres reports no long-running query on the primary; the deadlock is entirely inside the service's client pool.

The reporting service started returning 500 on /v2/summary at 11:52. Every stack trace ends in summarize() on the same line, dereferencing a field the response mapper populates only when the account has an active subscription. Accounts created after the migration have the field present but null rather than absent, which the guard does not cover.

The export worker dies mid-job and the job is never retried, because the exception escapes the worker's handler and the broker sees the connection close rather than a nack. Logs show an unhandled TypeError in the CSV writer when a column contains an embedded newline. Roughly 3% of exports fail, matching the share of datasets containing one.

API gateway request latency spiked to 8s on every request path at 16:20, including paths with no downstream call. CPU on the gateway pods went to the limit. The only change was a WAF rule added ten minutes earlier containing a regex with nested quantifiers, evaluated against every request URI. Rolling the rule back restores 12ms.

After the config rollout every order-service instance connected to the staging database instead of production. The symptom was silent: writes succeeded, into the wrong place. The ConfigMap key that should hold the primary JDBC URL holds the staging one; a rename during the rollout left the old key in place and the application reads the old key first.

The one-click checkout button disappeared from the storefront for all users at 08:00. No deploy ran. The flag service shows flag 'one_click_checkout' flipped to false at 07:59 by a scheduled job that was supposed to flip a different flag; a copy-paste left the same key in both job definitions.
samples.annotationNote: Re-annotated from `checkout-ui`, which the incident text never carries. The text names two deployed workloads -- `storefront`, whose user-visible surface broke, and the `flag service`, where the misconfiguration lives. `checkout-ui` is neither; it was inferred from the symptom rather than read from the text, so grading against it measured the annotator rather than the model (finding 75, finding 78). `storefront` is the workload whose breakage is the incident, which is what the component rule states.

samples.incidentText: The pricing service returned 502 on 60% of requests for 18 minutes. Every failure is an upstream tax-calculation call answering 503; the pricing service's own error rate against all other dependencies is zero. The tax provider's status page shows a degradation window that matches exactly. Nothing in the pricing service's own resources moved.

The shipping service failed to start after the image rebuild. The client library bumped from 2.x to 3.x and the retry option moved from a top-level field into a nested policy object, so construction throws on an unknown option. The failure is deterministic and reproduces in a clean namespace with the same image.

The analytics dashboard showed yesterday's totals for four hours this morning. Reads go to a replica whose relay log position fell 40 minutes behind the primary. The primary is healthy; a bulk backfill on the primary is generating write volume the replica's single applier thread cannot match. Reads on the primary are current.

At 04:12 the image builder began failing every build with 'no space left on device' while df reported 40 percent used. The writable overlay had hit its 10Gi ephemeral limit: each build leaves a layer cache under /var/lib/buildkit, and the janitor that trims it runs on a schedule that a long build queue had outrun. Deleting the cache by hand restored builds until the queue grew again.

The ingest writer was OOMKilled twice overnight. It requests 1Gi but the JVM starts without a heap cap, so under a backlog it grows to whatever the node will give and the kernel reclaims it. Requesting 1Gi while using 3Gi also made the scheduler pack two copies onto one node. Setting the heap to 700m removed both the kills and the double packing.

After the overlay was rebuilt, catalog service requests larger than about 1,400 bytes started hanging while its health checks stayed green. Small payloads were unaffected. Captures show the handshake and the first data segment arriving and nothing after it, and a router on the new path reports dropping fragments. Lowering the interface MTU to 1,380 made every call complete.

The notification worker has not served a single request since the last rollout. Its container never gets past start-up: the entrypoint waits for a file the new image no longer creates, so it exits after twenty seconds and the kubelet backs off. No probe ever runs. Rolling the image back to the previous tag starts it immediately.

Every deploy of the webhook dispatcher drops about 300 deliveries. The process handles the termination signal by closing its listener but keeps draining an internal queue for up to two minutes, and the pod is killed at thirty seconds, so the drain never finishes. A preStop hook that sleeps forty seconds, plus a longer grace period than the drain, made the drops disappear.

The product index served stale and missing entries for ninety minutes. Two of the sixteen cluster slots were unassigned: a node had been replaced and the cluster's replica placement pins a copy to a zone label the replacement does not carry. Reads against the surviving shards kept answering, which is why dashboards showed partial success rather than an outage. Adding the label let the cluster converge in four minutes.

The ledger writer's publishes began timing out at 21:40 and its producer buffer grew to 40,000 records. Broker logs show the disk watermark crossed 92 percent: the topic's retention was raised to seven days during the week and the broker volumes were sized for three. Producers were throttled rather than failed. Lowering retention to three days dropped the watermark and publishes resumed within a minute.

The invoice renderer skipped the last line of every multi-page invoice. The loop that splits items into pages advances its index by the page size after appending, so the item on the boundary is written to the current page and then skipped on the next one. Nothing is logged and totals still match, because the total is summed from the source list rather than from the rendered pages. Advancing by page size minus one restores every line.

Booking reminders went out an hour early for every appointment created after the daylight saving change. The API stores a local wall-clock time plus a zone name, then converts with a fixed offset read once at process start. Restarting the pods for an unrelated deploy hid it for a week, which is why the first report blamed the scheduler. Converting per request with the zone's rules for that date fixes it.

Partner portal uploads began failing with 504 for files over 5MB, immediately after an ingress change. The annotation that sets the upstream read timeout was written as 1s where the previous value was 600s, and the upload handler needs about eight seconds. Nothing in the application changed and its own logs show the work completing. Restoring the annotation to 600s fixed every failure.

Settlement totals were wrong by a few cents for two hours. The currency feed's response changed shape -- the rate object used to carry a single rate field and now carries rate plus inverse -- and the feed's own status page shows the change deployed at 09:00. Settlement's parser still reads the old field, which is now rounded. The feed team reverted at 11:00 and totals matched again.
